articles.title: Ancient cave art discovery suggests first known humans in Ireland walked over from Wales
articles.summary: During the most recent Ice Age, researchers believe there was a "lost land bridge" between Wales and Ireland.
articles.body:
Researchers believe the first known humans to set foot on Ireland thousands of years ago were most likely from Wales, following the "exciting" discovery of ancient cave art.

During the most recent Ice Age, when much of the British Isles were beneath a vast continental glacier, the depleted sea levels opened a "lost land bridge" between modern-day Pembrokeshire and the south-east tip of Ireland, around Rosslare.

According to rock expert Dr George Nash, from Liverpool University, the opportunities presented by this pathway would have been too good for hunter gatherers to ignore.

Now, alongside an international team of experts, Nash has located eight cave sites in south-west Ireland featuring rock art dating back from at least 15,000 years ago, around 5,000 years before the previous oldest example of humans in Ireland.

Nash, who coordinated the Lost Land Bridge Project alongside Genevieve von Petzinger and Barbara Oosterwijk, said there would have been a forested and grassland plateau around 46 miles (76 km) coast-to-coast.

With summertime temperatures typically -10°C to -20°C, Nash said the pathway would have supported wild horses, mammoth, bison, reindeer and other large herbivores, which fed off the hardy sedges, mosses and lichens growing through the fertile, but near-frozen soil.

Nash said he had always believed - from what he had gleaned throughout his career about human movement during the period - that it was inconceivable that people would not have utilised the opportunity the pathway presented.

This led him to assemble his multi-disciplinary team of experts from University College Dublin and the University of Adelaide, along with academics from Abu Dhabi, Wales and Portugal.

"Up until now the earliest evidence archaeologists had found - through accidental discovery - was from around 10,500 years ago, but everyone - not just me - knew that simply couldn't have been correct.

"We just weren't looking hard enough, and not in the right places. The principle we worked on was 'absence of proof isn't proof of absence'."

He said advances in artificial intelligence (AI) had been a game-changer.

"With the help of caving specialist Shane Diffily and digital mapping consultant Darren Lee, we were able to fill a computer algorithm with everything we knew about the characteristics of cave dwellings in south Wales and set it to work searching for similar sites in Ireland, without us trudging blindly around the countryside, hoping to bump into something which looked promising."

What their computer model spat out was 28 potential caves in south-west Ireland which the team investigated.

Eight of them were found to have cave art which they believe dates from at least 15,000 years ago and possibly much earlier, and around 5,000 years before the previous oldest example of humans in Ireland.

The team are currently unwilling to be more precise about the location of the caves, for fear that they may be vandalised or looted.

"We know that modern day south Wales was settled from around 35,000 to 40,000 years ago, by intrepid early modern humans from southern England, France and Spain, crossing the then dried-up land bridges of the English and Bristol Channels - seasonally settling in caves along the inhabitable strip of land stretching from Chepstow to St Davids," said Nash.

"Over 20,000 years their art progressed from primitive line drawings which may have been early tally charts, to more figurative and representative depictions of the world around them, and what we've found in Ireland is yet another progression from that."

The rock art which the Lost Land Bridge Project has uncovered includes engravings on the cave walls, paintings in ochre and charcoal and line sketches indented into clay and earth by fingertips.

Nash believes the growing population put pressure on humans to move ever more west and northwards.

"There were around 100 human-inhabited caves on The Gower Peninsula for example, in a time when the technology didn't yet exist for human groups to create their own free-standing dwellings."

Nash said the caves would have been "quite a cosy place to live, especially compared with the -20°C outside".

"Competition for these caves would have been intense," he added.

"As family networks grew, knowledge of how to survive by following animal migration routes improved and they must have become bolder."

The Lost Land Bridge Project team believe the potential for more future discoveries is high.

"The sites we've currently explored are in south-west Ireland, but it's illogical to presume that early humans just bypassed Wexford, Waterford and Cork, and ploughed on west," said Nash.

"There must be more, and even earlier places which are just waiting for us to find them. This project is now pushing the boundaries of what we consider to be the final vestiges of a north-west European frontier. It's all very exciting."

articles.title: How melting Arctic glaciers is creating a climate ‘doom loop'
articles.summary: The more glaciers melt, the more of the greenhouse gas they are likely to release into the atmosphere. The post How melting Arctic glaciers is creating a cli...
articles.body:
Melting Arctic glaciers are releasing ancient methane from rocks beneath the ice, creating a natural feedback loop that may worsen as the region continues to warm.

Research conducted in Svalbard reveals that glacier meltwater rivers are carrying methane from rocks under the ice into the atmosphere, with every river tested containing more methane than expected.

The study estimates that land-terminating glaciers across Svalbard may transport between 182 to 368 metric tons of methane per year in meltwater, highlighting a previously undercounted pathway for ancient carbon to reach the atmosphere.

Melting Arctic glaciers are creating a climate "doom loop" by flushing out ancient methane from rocks beneath the ice, reveals new research.

The more glaciers melt, the more of the greenhouse gas they are likely to release into the atmosphere, say scientists.

The study shows meltwater rivers flowing from Svalbard glaciers inside the Arctic Circle are carrying ancient methane from rocks under the ice into the open air

The findings reveal a natural "feedback" loop that scientists warn may worsen as the Arctic continues to get warmer.

They say melting glaciers can open hidden pathways for the powerful greenhouse gas.

The study, published in the journal Nature Communications , was led by Gabrielle Kleber from the iC3 Polar Research Hub in Tromsø, Norway.

Her team sampled rivers draining valley glaciers across Svalbard.

They found methane in every river they tested.

The research team took 148 water samples from 19 glacier-fed rivers in central Svalbard, providing the most extensive assessment yet of methane in glacier meltwater in the region.

Every river in their survey contained more methane than expected from contact with the atmosphere, with the highest values reaching up to 425 times that level.

Study co-author Silje Waaler says the team deliberately designed the survey to capture the diversity of glaciers across the region.

She said: "We wanted to study many different glaciers, across a range of rock types and ice conditions.

"That gave us a clearer picture of why some glacier rivers carry more methane than others.

A key finding was that the methane is mostly not being made by microbes under the ice, as has been observed beneath glaciers in Greenland.

Instead, it appears to come from Svalbard's geology.

Many parts of the archipelago contain old shale layers rich in organic carbon.

Over millions of years, heat and pressure can turn the material into methane and other gases.

They also analyzed the carbon in the methane to identify its source.

In some samples, they measured related gases - including ethane and propane - which helped confirm that much of the methane came from geological sources.

Kleber said: "These glaciers are mostly melting on their surfaces.

"But this meltwater finds its way to the bottom of the glaciers through crevasses and holes.

"This means that it interacts with the rocks underneath, and where those rocks contain ancient gas, the water can flush methane out into rivers."

She said the most methane-rich waters came from glaciers resting on shale-bearing rock formations, but geology alone did not explain everything.

The team also found that the physical state of the glacier bed matters.

Glaciers with thawed, wet and active beds were far better at picking up methane.

Glaciers frozen to their beds were less connected to the rocks below, even when methane-rich geology was present.

To understand the processes, the research team combined river chemistry with ice surveys.

They used ground-penetrating radar to map ice conditions within selected glaciers.

That allowed them to estimate how much of each glacier bed was thawed and able to carry water.

Co-author Leonard Magerl, a doctoral candidate, said: "The temperature at the base of glaciers is an important piece of the puzzle.

"We found that the biggest methane releases happened where the right rocks and the right glacier conditions came together.

"This insight can help to estimate emissions from other ice-covered regions."

The research team estimates that land-terminating glaciers across Svalbard may transport between around 182 to 368 metric tons of methane per year in meltwater, depending on how the estimate is scaled.

That is in addition to previous, much higher estimates for methane released by groundwater springs in front of glaciers.

But the researchers say it still points to a widespread and undercounted pathway for ancient carbon to reach the atmosphere.

While the study focused on Svalbard, the team believes similar methane-release pathways likely occur in other glaciated regions where ice overlies organic-rich rocks or sediments - including large parts of the Arctic, the Himalayas and Antarctica .

Kleber said: "The amounts reported here are small compared with human-caused emissions from fossil fuels, farming and waste.

"But they matter because they reveal a natural feedback loop that is not confined to Svalbard, and that may grow as the Arctic warms ."

As glaciers thin and retreat, she says more meltwater may reach their beds whch can increase contact with fractured rock, sediment and groundwater.

In some places, that may flush out more methane.

Kleber said some Svalbard glaciers are also becoming colder at their beds as they shrink.

If a glacier becomes frozen to its bed, she said its ability to flush methane through subglacial rivers may fall.

Kleber added: "Our results show that future methane release will depend on both geology and glacier change.

"That makes it important to know what lies beneath the ice, not only how fast the ice is melting."

Kleber and Magerl have previously found that meltwater from one Svalbard glacier could carry geologic methane from beneath the ice, making it release more methane per area than Greenland glaciers.

But newly uncovered groundwater springs are also releasing the potent greenhouse gas in Svalbard.

The new study shows that methane-rich meltwater is not unique to one glacier, but is widespread across central Svalbard being strongest where shale-rich geology and thawed glacier beds overlap.
